title: Bills film review: Is Buffalo headed for a shootout against the Lions? Joe Buscaglia 30
summary:
Greg Rousseau was a bright spot on defense in Buffalo’s season-opening win, particularly when rushing from the defensive left side. Alex Slitz / Getty Images
The Buffalo Bills kicked off the Joe Brady era with a rousing win over the Houston Texans, but the defense remains the biggest question mark as Thursday’s game against the Detroit Lions looms on a short week.
Here’s a position-by-position review of what stood out on defense, and what the Bills might need to do to fix it for Thursday. Plus,
full_text:
Greg Rousseau was a bright spot on defense in Buffalo’s season-opening win, particularly when rushing from the defensive left side. Alex Slitz / Getty Images
The Buffalo Bills kicked off the Joe Brady era with a rousing win over the Houston Texans, but the defense remains the biggest question mark as Thursday’s game against the Detroit Lions looms on a short week.
Here’s a position-by-position review of what stood out on defense, and what the Bills might need to do to fix it for Thursday. Plus, our Week 1 grades, projected Week 2 Bills inactives and a prediction for Bills versus Lions.
How it looked on film: Ed Oliver and Deone Walker were excellent against the Texans. Oliver played a massive snap share and did a lot of little things to help free up his teammates, while continuing to be a nuisance in one-on-ones. Walker played slightly less than Oliver, coming off the field when the Bills went into their dime formations.
As a run defender, Walker could shed blocks and create pressure while holding his ground against a double team. He was also a great pass rusher from his position. His best rep was when he sniffed out a screen outside the hashmarks and immediately brought down the receiver.
Outlook versus the Lions: Above all, the Bills should use Walker more and maybe Oliver less. Walker looks like a perfect fit for this defensive scheme and the principles the Bills want to play with. It could be worth their time to give Walker dime reps instead of Oliver to give Walker more time on the field and Oliver more rest. If T.J. Sanders can play (knee, illness), they might want him to take some reps Landon Jackson had, since Jackson struggled in Week 1.
How it looked on film: Greg Rousseau looked better on film than he did in the game. His usual prominence as a run defender carried over for the most part, but in the pass rush, the Bills empowered Rousseau the way they haven’t in a few seasons. I’ve been a broken record about this for a few years, but given the results and how Rousseau looked in Week 1, the Bills agreed he is at his best rushing from the defensive left side against the right tackle.
The Bills had him line up on the right side occasionally on early downs, as he and Bradley Chubb decided once the Texans lined up and they saw the strong and weak sides. But in clear passing situations, Rousseau lined up on the defensive left side, which plays to his strengths as a pass rusher and made him a threat to get into the backfield.
Chubb was a slight disappointment in his Bills debut from a pass-rushing perspective. He had a handful of good reps, but the left tackle mostly washed him out in the matchup. Chubb was generally where he needed to be, which has value, but he wasn’t particularly impactful.
Outlook versus the Lions: The Bills should keep everything the same with Rousseau: his snap share, where they’re lining him up and, specifically, having him rush against the right tackle in passing situations.
If there was one thing to consider, it would be to sub Chubb out more to keep him fresher. I thought T.J. Parker showed some nice pass-rushing reps and mostly rushed from Chubb’s side (the right). Although there were some inconsistencies in Parker’s overall game, there was enough there to warrant a handful of more snaps.
How it looked on film: It wasn’t the massive problem some made it out to be, but the inside linebacker room still had key deficiencies in Week 1. Terrel Bernard, who entered the game fully healthy, showed more success getting past blocks. He usually did so by dipping under the block attempt rather than stacking and shedding, but he stayed cleaner than he did in 2025. When the blocker got hands on him, however, he struggled to shed the block. A couple of times, he was too hesitant in firing forward against the run, too.
Dorian Williams played most of the snaps, but there were multiple hang-ups in pass coverage. On the David Montgomery touchdown catch, the Bills looked to be in man coverage, and Williams was lined up over Montgomery. As Montgomery headed to the opposite side of the formation, it looked as if Williams tried to pass him off to someone, but everyone else had an assignment. The Bills tried rookie Kaleb Elarms-Orr in a handful of passing situations, though it was short-lived. The rookie was pulled after Jaylin Noel caught a 35-yard pass with no one around in the middle of the field, suggesting a blown assignment.
Outlook versus the Lions: The Bills are in a difficult spot at inside linebacker, with no clear short-term path forward for Week 2. Their long-term hope is that Elarms-Orr develops enough to become the starter, as he has the best potential blend of run defending, block shedding and holding his own in coverage, but he may not be ready yet. In the meantime, they’ll hope for more from Bernard as a run defender and to help build a game plan that helps Williams in coverage. Until Elarms-Orr is ready, there could be volatile moments. If Bernard (calf) can’t play, it means questions at both inside linebacker spots.
How it looked on film: Top cornerback Christian Benford had a rough start, shadowing Nico Collins all game. The Bills tried to speed up quarterback C.J. Stroud early in the contest with pressure packages, and the Texans quarterback did a great job of getting the ball out quickly. It left Benford in tough spots, and it didn’t go well early.
After the Bills adjusted to focus more on coverage in the second half, however, I thought Benford was excellent. He looked good in man coverage in a tough matchup and helped give the Bills’ front the time to get in the backfield.
The other cornerback spots are more concerning. The Texans didn’t test No. 2 cornerback Maxwell Hairston much, but he surrendered too much space on multiple reps. The Bills also had a near disaster at the end of the game, as Hairston froze in his assignment and allowed Noel to get behind him, setting the Texans up with a first-and-goal from the 9-yard line with the game on the line. If C.J. Gardner-Johnson hadn’t played a hunch and gotten to Noel to push him out of bounds, Hairston’s error easily could have decided the game.
Hairston also had good man-coverage reps, though. Rookie boundary cornerback Davison Igbinosun had some good reps, but he was pulled from the game mid-drive in his second series, potentially indicating an assignment error. Nickel Dee Alford struggled a few times in man coverage, too.
Outlook versus the Lions: With so many dangerous pass-catching assets for the Lions, the cornerbacks will be tested often. Given the Lions’ overall boundary speed, it wouldn’t be a surprise if the Bills go with Hairston fully in this game, despite the flaws he showed against the Texans.
Igbinosun trying to turn and run with Jameson Williams seems like an illogical choice the Bills should avoid if they can. Amon-Ra St. Brown is a matchup nightmare for their entire secondary. Given the opponent, it could be a heavy zone game with a little man coverage sprinkled in, but it’s a tough matchup through and through.
How it looked on film: Cole Bishop was solid but unspectacular; Gardner-Johnson played hunches and had some good ones, but he was out of position on others. The big issue of the day was Damar Hamlin, a notable weakness when the Bills put him in for dime coverage.
Hamlin’s lack of athleticism is offset by him lining up farther back, which gives more space underneath and creates more catch opportunities. Including penalties, the Bills’ third-down defense gave up first downs on more than half of the Texans’ chances, and Hamlin played a big role. One week in, and the Bills may have some growing pains with this group, though Bishop seems well suited to the scheme and should have far better days.
Outlook versus the Lions: Bishop’s injuries (knee, groin) are something to monitor. If he cannot play, it could force Hamlin into the starting lineup, unless they go with Jordan Hancock or Jalon Kilgore or even consider starting nickel Dee Alford there.
If…

title: Ben Johnson-Brian Flores showdown could set course for season in competitive NFC North The pregame planning and in-game adaptations of Johnson and Flores should be one of the highlights of the Vikings-Bears matchup in Week 2. Alec Lewis 17

full_text:
The matchup between Bears coach Ben Johnson and Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores should be one of the highlights of the teams' Week 2 clash in Chicago. Michael Reaves and Luke Hales / Getty Images
Two years ago, in the lead-up to one of these clashes, a reporter coaxed a smile out of then-Detroit Lions offensive coordinator Ben Johnson.
The reporter had asked about Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores’ blitz packages. How, the reporter wondered, did the relentless pressure tax players’ minds? Johnson, steely as ever, listened to the full question.
“Yeah, um …” Johnson said before chuckling.
His initial reaction carried a tinge of mischief. It felt like the reaction of a poker shark at a hold ’em table. The type of response you’d have about an opponent you know is always up to something.
The reporter followed up on the initial question, citing a compliment from Flores about Johnson’s abilities. How flattering was that to hear?
“I think he’s trying to just butter us up a little bit,” Johnson said.
He smirked once more, another brief window into a vaunted back-and-forth that returns this weekend. Johnson is now the head coach of the Chicago Bears, and for the seventh time, these two foes will meet in a critical NFC North matchup.
Winning offers far more than just bragging rights. The victor will establish solid footing in a divisional race that’s likely to be decided down the stretch.
It simplifies the nuances of any matchup to pit two play callers against each other. This, though, is a special case. Johnson’s offense represents creativity and detail, born from a self-made coaching career. Flores’ defense embodies a trademark fearlessness. The Vikings don’t blitz because it’s flashy or because it produces eye-popping graphics. They send waves of bodies at offenses from all sides because that’s what they think is most likely to produce the right result.
Johnson has publicly stated his preference for points and blowouts. Flores makes no bones about his desire to apply a vise grip to opposing offenses. Neither settles for satisfaction. Both recognize the challenge the other presents.
“They do a great job,” Flores said Tuesday afternoon. “There’s shifts, there’s motions, there’s a lot of eye candy. They do everything that could potentially give a defense problems.”
He even offered a window into how his mind might work Sunday at Soldier Field. Employ one deep safety, and Chicago’s wideouts may feast against man-to-man coverage. Shift and feature two deep safeties, and the Bears could find susceptibilities in Minnesota’s ability to stop the run.
And that’s only the tip of the iceberg.
Safety positioning matters, but so do protection rules and pre-snap signals and down-and-distance tendencies. Each coverage choice comes with a cost. Different run concepts open the door to holes. All avenues of communication matter because they could contain the key for either side to decipher the deception.
As former Vikings defensive lineman Harrison Phillips put it several years ago, playing Johnson is like navigating a volatile stock market. You enter with expectations, but every drive seems like a forecasting exercise. Does it make sense to sell off while ahead? Should Minnesota adjust schematically even if the team is succeeding? Or does it make sense to stick with the investment? Should Minnesota maintain its approach, betting against Chicago’s ability to find a quick answer?
The shared history only adds to the complexity of the decisions.
“Each week, you try to find a weakness in the armor and look to attack it,” Johnson said ahead of the highly anticipated Vikings-Lions bout in Week 18 of the 2024 season. “This defense doesn’t have much, and it’s been that way for two years now. You can tell that this whole unit has been together. They have the answers. They know how to respond when they get hit with something.”
Going back to Johnson and Flores’ first faceoffs in 2023, a visual breakdown of the quarter-by-quarter efficiency statistics looks like a round-by-round scoring of Hagler-Hearns. Throwing the uppercut is less important than being able to absorb one.
In the Week 7 confrontation between Johnson’s Lions and Flores’ Vikings in 2024, Minnesota limited Detroit to a minuscule 21.4 percent success rate in the first quarter. Detroit answered with a ridiculous 61.1 percent success rate in the second quarter. The Lions kept their momentum with a 54.5 percent success rate in the third quarter, but the Vikings eliminated the rhythm by holding them to a 27.8 percent success rate in the fourth.
Detroit won 31-29, but the lopsided blow-by-blow revealed the ingenuity of their staffs and players.
Both coaches worked with a collective to identify and solve problems on the fly. This takes sharp eyes from above, intricate sideline dialogue and shrewd on-field adaptation.
“Any type of offense that’s out there — ground and pound, run and shoot, RPO, 4 by 1 — he’s got it,” Flores said. “So what are we getting this week? It’s hard to know. A lot of the game is adjustments. If they do this, we want to do this. We’re going to have our own game plan, and it’s the same on his end with him asking, ‘What are they doing? How are we going to counteract it?’”
Last year against Flores, Johnson utilized condensed formations, quick snaps and third-down runs at a notable clip. Flores, meanwhile, kept his max-pressure calls to a minimum against Johnson. He also deployed mostly zone coverage out of heavier personnel to neutralize the Bears’ run-pass multiplicity.
Also like poker players, they understand the others’ preferences. They know what moves the other prefers to make on the field.
“It’s one of the things I love about coaching defense in this division in the NFC,” Flores said. “It’s a lot of fun.”
It’s fun to watch, as well.

full_text:
Bears quarterback Caleb Williams ran 10 times for 65 yards and two touchdowns against the Panthers on Sunday. Jared C. Tilton / Getty Images
For the past two-and-a-half days, Chicago has been in a state of euphoria because of the Bears offense. Fifty-nine points in a season opener? In a performance where room for improvement on offense remains quite obvious?
This can’t be real, can it?
By this point, the recap of Sunday’s 59-37 thumping of the Carolina Panthers has centered primarily on all the big plays from quarterback Caleb Williams, running back D’Andre Swift and their offensive mates.
This was, after all, a convincing victory that announced — or maybe reaffirmed? — the Bears as a legitimately dangerous team in the NFC. But the path to 1-0 included a little bit of everything Sunday in Charlotte, N.C. Timely takeaways. Big momentum shifts. Fortunate breaks.
Forget about those eight touchdowns the Bears scored for a minute. Here are four less obvious moments that mattered Sunday in an encouraging road win.
Williams’ 29-yard touchdown sprint in the final minute before halftime matched his career-long run, a similar scramble in a fourth-quarter rally against the New York Giants last season.
Williams also had a 9-yard TD run in the first quarter Sunday. But an argument can be made that his first rush of the afternoon — a 6-yard scramble for a first down — offered the ideal example of how dangerous he can be on the move.
Feeling heat in the pocket, Williams was able to shuffle and escape. And as he rolled right, he kept his eyes downfield with the threat of a pass alive. That froze Carolina cornerback Mike Jackson.
Williams, meanwhile, cruised gracefully to his right with outside linebacker Jeremiah Moon closing in. Then he turned on the jets at just the right moment and with impressive acceleration to pick up a first down.
Of the quarterback’s six scramble runs, four moved the chains.
Bears coaches continually remind their quarterback just how dangerous his speed is . And so a handful of times every game, expect Williams to put that to use with a sharp understanding of when and how to turn scramble-and-throw hopes into tuck-and-run opportunities.
As for Williams’ long TD run just before halftime Sunday? It seems like he knew he would score when he was still all the way back at the 30 and had emerged from the trash heap in the backfield.
“I got through (it) and I saw a lot of space,” he said. “I saw no ’backers, so I didn’t have to weave through anybody. And the third-level defenders were manned up and plastering our guys. So from there, it was just beat them to the pylon. … Just finding little ways to help the team.”
The punches were going back and forth Sunday like a “Rocky” scene, with both the Bears and Panthers landing big blows during a chaotic first half. Early in the second quarter, the Bears found themselves against the ropes.
First came a failed quarterback sneak on fourth-and-1 from the Chicago 21, a risky call by Johnson that he would have been skewered for all week had his team lost. The Panthers quickly turned that stop into a three-play touchdown drive to tie the game at 21, then forced a three-and-out.
No better time for the “banana ball,” with Bears punter Tory Taylor thumping a slicing 48-yard punt with significant spin and a tricky trajectory. That’s something the Bears believed all week could offer them a boost. And it certainly did when Panthers returner Jimmy Horn Jr. muffed his fair-catch attempt.
Kaden Davis, a preseason standout who was activated from the practice squad Saturday, was there for the recovery, a big play that allowed the Bears to steal three points even without squeezing a first down out of the ensuing possession.
Cairo Santos’ 40-yard field goal provided a 24-21 lead and the Bears never trailed again.
“A huge momentum swing,” Johnson said.
Throughout the spring and summer, Johnson hammered his team on the importance of being sharp at the ends of halves. As good as the Bears were with end-of-game situations in 2025, they were too frequently clunky, careless and unproductive before halftime.
That became a major emphasis, with ample on-field situational work used during training camp to sharpen the Bears’ mindset and execution for the final minutes before halftime .
Test 1 in Carolina: the Bears closed Sunday’s first half with a touchdown and a takeaway.
Williams’ 29-yard scoring scramble finished a drive that had been set back initially by a 6-yard sack on the first play and later by a delay-of-game penalty — coming out of a timeout.
No matter. Williams and his troops got themselves back on track and finished the way Johnson wants. “That was huge,” the Bears coach said. “It was good to see.”
Two snaps later, rookie cornerback Malik Muhammad met his coach’s demand of eliminating a “retaliatory score,” contributing a diving interception on a Bryce Young pass to receiver Jalen Coker.
Said Muhammad: “Man, I felt great after that interception. I’m not going to lie.”
Truth be told, the rookie may have felt great emotionally. But his first NFL pick ended with him landing right on top of the football, losing his breath and needing a moment to gather himself.
“The ball knocked the wind out of me,” Muhammad said. “I was wishing it didn’t. Because I had a good celebration planned.”
With the game tied at 31 late in the third quarter, tight end Colston Loveland was flagged for a holding penalty in the red zone. That pushed the Bears back into a second-and-20 situation from the Carolina 21. That could have been a drive killer had the Panthers not reciprocated with a costly penalty of their own.
Instead, on a passing play that went haywire, Williams shuffled and skittered and scrambled, retreating 25 yards behind the line of scrimmage before throwing the ball out of bounds. The football was out of his hand for a half-second when Carolina defensive end Derrick Brown took an extra step and drilled the Bears quarterback.
Roughing the passer. Fifteen yards. Free first down.
Ultimately, that was a brutal mistake by Brown, especially so far behind the line of scrimmage. But it provided a huge boost to the Bears on a drive that ended with the second of Swift’s three touchdowns for a 38-31 lead.
Indeed, the NFL’s best teams find a way to squeeze the maximum gain out of their good fortune. And the Bears, with Williams at the wheel, are showing consistent ability to do just that.
Brown’s second penalty two possessions later — this one an offside infraction — negated his interception of a batted Williams pass in the end zone. One snap later, Williams hit receiver Jahdae Walker for a 1-yard score.

full_text:
Alex Singleton's missed tackle on Emmett Johnson was one of many in the Broncos' loss to the Chiefs on Monday. Jamie Squire / Getty Images
Denver Broncos linebacker Alex Singleton, in the days leading up to his team’s season opener in Kansas City, explained the unique challenge the Kansas City Chiefs would pose with new running back Kenneth Walker III.
“He really takes the ball anywhere on the field on any given play,” Singleton said. “You can’t just, like, on a stretch play, set the front side. You have to have containment on the backside, and really all over, and force the 11 guys on defense to be able to tackle him.”
Give the Broncos an A for identifying the specificity of the challenge … and an F for executing in the face of it.
Nothing about what the Chiefs chose to do against Denver’s defense in Monday night’s opener surprised the Broncos. Perhaps that’s what made the unit’s inept performance in the 31-10 loss — 220 rushing yards allowed, 28 missed tackles — all the more discouraging. This wasn’t the 2008 Miami Dolphins unveiling the wildcat out of nowhere to run all over Bill Belichick’s New England Patriots. The Chiefs didn’t pay Walker a contract worth up to $15 million per year not to feature him heavily, especially as Patrick Mahomes was making his return just nine months after an ACL tear.
“When you do go get a back like that,” Singleton said ahead of the matchup, “it is saying to the league, the entire NFL, ‘Hey, we want to run the ball. We’re going to show the league that we can.’”
The sheer volume of missed tackles when the Broncos were trying to bring down Walker — or essentially any other Chiefs player with the ball in his hands — was staggering, but it wasn’t an entirely new problem. Denver ranked No. 1 last season in the NFL in opponent yards per rush before contact by a wide margin (0.72 yards), according to TruMedia. It was only 22nd, though, in yards per rush after contact (3.15). Though that’s not an exact reflection of missed tackles — a running back can be wrapped up by a defender and still fall forward for 1 or 2 yards, for example — it illustrates a vulnerability teams with committed rushing attacks have increasingly been able to exploit. The Broncos in the three games since the start of last year’s playoffs (Buffalo Bills, Patriots, Chiefs) have allowed 181 rushing yards per game.
If that becomes a full-blown trend, it will be hard for the Broncos to engage a pass rush teams are already going to great lengths to mitigate. Mahomes on Monday, for example, released the ball at an average of 2.27 seconds after the snap, the quickest time to throw in any of his career games against the Broncos, according to Next Gen Stats. If that becomes the norm for Broncos opponents, Denver will have to walk a tightrope to produce any kind of winning formula from there.
“It’s really correctable, so that’s the good news,” defensive end Zach Allen said as he spoke to reporters on a conference call Tuesday afternoon. “It’s definitely going to be a point of emphasis in practice this week. Knowing the guys we’ve got in the group, it will get addressed, and it will get fixed. It shouldn’t be a problem anymore.”
The Broncos across the 2024 and 2025 seasons ranked first in opponent rushing yards allowed per attempt (3.9) and fourth in defensive expected points added per game on opponents’ designed rushes, according to TruMedia. So Allen is right when he suggests the Broncos have a history of defending the run at a high level they can point to as they try to make corrections. Still, the performance of Denver’s defense in the opener can’t simply be brushed away. There were too many concerning images to suggest Denver has an iron-wall run defense that was simply on the fritz for one night.
Singleton, the 32-year-old whom the Broncos re-signed to a two-year contract extension this offseason, was charged with five missed tackles alone Monday night, according to Next Gen Stats, the highest total in a single game in his career. The Broncos pushed the Chiefs into a third-and-5 as the fourth quarter began. Denver trailed, 24-10, and still had a chance to get back into the game as Mahomes took the snap at the Broncos’ 29-yard line. The quarterback hit rookie running back Emmett Johnson in the flat, and Singleton made the beeline to the ball, only to be stiff-armed to the ground by the powerful young ball carrier. Whether it’s those extended looks in the mirror, personnel adjustments or schematic tweaks, the Broncos must get a literal grasp on their opponents’ ball carriers. It’s the only way to eliminate concern recent results against the run are becoming an extended trend.

full_text:
Jordan Love was under pressure throughout Sunday's loss to the Vikings. Jeffrey Becker / Imagn Images
GREEN BAY, Wis. — Green Bay Packers offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich was asked Tuesday what he tells his players when quarterback Jordan Love gets hit 15 times in a game, as statistics indicate he did in Week 1 against the Minnesota Vikings.
“Eighteen times, actually,” Stenavich said. “It’s not good enough. It’s not the standard. That’s not what we’re going to be about. We’ve got to be better.”
Stenavich, who coached Green Bay’s offensive line from 2019-2021 before becoming offensive coordinator in 2022, attributed the pass protection shortcomings against a familiar opponent and coordinator to miscommunications and mental breakdowns. There were physical deficiencies, too, and they all combined to produce a dreadful day at the office for a team that couldn’t protect its quarterback in a 39-22 loss.
The Vikings’ 54.3 pressure percentage is first in the NFL after one week, per TruMedia. They blitzed on 73.9 percent of Packers dropbacks. No other team blitzed on more than 46 percent of its opponent’s dropbacks. Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores normally blitzes a lot — their 47.1 percent blitz rate last season was first in the NFL by almost 14 percentage points — but this was another level. Flores thought he could take advantage of a Packers offensive line with pressing questions at four of five spots. At times, he did that and then some.
Stenavich logged 18 quarterback hits, but TruMedia’s 15 for Minnesota were still six more than any other team in Week 1. Their average time to pressure of 2.38 seconds ranked fifth.
Interestingly, the Vikings’ pressure percentage was higher when they didn’t blitz (58.3 percent, more than 14 percentage points higher than any other team’s pressure percentage when not blitzing) than when they did (52.9 percent, 11th in the NFL). Love was one of the league’s best against the blitz last season and found success against it in the first half last Sunday, but the Vikings had four sacks and an interception when blitzing in the second half, per Next Gen Stats.
“I felt like as far as guys knowing what to do going into a game plan, I felt pretty good with all of that stuff,” Stenavich said. “But again, when you get into those environments, it’s just a good learning tool for everybody of how important it is to just be on top of your communication in those hostile environments. So we’ve just got to learn from it and get better.
“I said it last week in my press conference that this was going to be probably the toughest environment that we were going to play in, mixed with all the pressures and different communication things we’re going to have to face. … I’m not going to freak out or overreact or anything like that. This is the first game of a 17-game season.”
No matter what numbers you look at, Green Bay’s pass protection, which includes running backs and tight ends in addition to offensive linemen, was bad. Really bad. The Packers also need to run the ball better (3.1 yards per carry in Week 1), as Stenavich said the best pass protection is running the ball effectively. That would keep defenses on their toes more and keep the Packers out of as many obvious passing situations.
So what happens next as the Packers prepare to visit the New York Jets in Week 2?
For one, the offensive line might not look the same. Stenavich said they’ll rotate a few guys in practice this week to determine who the best five are. That answer was in response to a question about whether Anthony Belton is in play at guard. Belton, the Packers’ 2025 second-round pick, started seven games at right guard last season before losing the job this summer to Jacob Monk, in part because he was poor in pass protection.
Belton worked more at backup right tackle as Zach Bako-Bewele eased back from offseason knee surgery, but Belton might not be needed there as much now that Bako-Bewele is situated. If you’re asking why the Packers are already weighing changes to the offensive line after one game, and if so, why they settled on the line they trotted out against the Vikings in the first place, those are fair questions.
Jordan Morgan was always going to play left tackle, and Stenavich said Tuesday of the 2024 first-round pick, “I think he could be better, and he will be. There were some plays I think he would like to have back, but again, it’s the first game of the year, and we’ve just got to make sure we’re improving with our technique and everything like that.”
The most controversial decision was starting Donovan Jennings at left guard over rookie fifth-round pick Jager Burton, who appeared to be above Jennings on the summer depth chart. Head coach Matt LaFleur said Jennings had more time on task this offseason and did a nice job, while Stenavich said Jennings played better in practice the last couple of weeks. The solution there is for Aaron Banks to get healthy. The Packers signed him to a four-year, $77 million deal in free agency last year, but injuries hampered his debut season in Green Bay. He was solid when healthy at the end of the season, but a knee injury limited him in camp, and despite practicing in a limited capacity all last week, Banks missed another game.
Sean Rhyan signed an extension to be the center this offseason, so that wasn’t up in the air, and Monk won the right guard job over Belton this summer, in part because coaches liked his nasty playstyle. Bako-Bewele is an elite right tackle when healthy, and he’s clearly working back to form after an uneven camp upon returning from injury.
“I thought coming back, dealing with what he’s been dealing with, it was a plus from what I wanted,” Stenavich said of Bako-Bewele. “He hadn’t gotten a lot of reps in practice and things like that. He made it through the game. He battled. Was it his best game? No, but I think there’s a lot he can build on, and I expect him, as the season rolls through, for him to be playing some pretty high-level ball pretty soon.”
The Packers have rotated offensive linemen in the past, but LaFleur said Monday they need to find continuity up front as quickly as possible. That might be more of a commentary on the lack of clean health up front since camp started in late July, so getting Banks back is paramount.
“I think that’s part of the problem, is we’ve had a lot of guys in and out of the lineup,” LaFleur said. “I’m not making excuses. It is what it is. You’ve got to find a way to get it done, but I do think the more guys play together, typically the better they play together.”
The Packers won’t see pressure looks like they did on Sunday, except for when the Vikings visit Lambeau Field in two months, but Stenavich said he “absolutely” expects opposing defenses to heat up the Packers more until they prove they can handle it. It wasn’t all bad, especially when Love threw for 189 yards and two touchdowns when blitzed in the first half, but the Packers can’t afford to crumble up front as often as they did, and that starts with a chance at redemption against the Jets on Sunday.

summary:

full_text:
The matchup between Bears coach Ben Johnson and Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores should be one of the highlights of the teams' Week 2 clash in Chicago. Michael Reaves and Luke Hales / Getty Images
Two years ago, in the lead-up to one of these clashes, a reporter coaxed a smile out of then-Detroit Lions offensive coordinator Ben Johnson.
The reporter had asked about Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores’ blitz packages. How, the reporter wondered, did the relentless pressure tax players’ minds? Johnson, steely as ever, listened to the full question.
“Yeah, um …” Johnson said before chuckling.
His initial reaction carried a tinge of mischief. It felt like the reaction of a poker shark at a hold ’em table. The type of response you’d have about an opponent you know is always up to something.
The reporter followed up on the initial question, citing a compliment from Flores about Johnson’s abilities. How flattering was that to hear?
“I think he’s trying to just butter us up a little bit,” Johnson said.
He smirked once more, another brief window into a vaunted back-and-forth that returns this weekend. Johnson is now the head coach of the Chicago Bears, and for the seventh time, these two foes will meet in a critical NFC North matchup.
Winning offers far more than just bragging rights. The victor will establish solid footing in a divisional race that’s likely to be decided down the stretch.
It simplifies the nuances of any matchup to pit two play callers against each other. This, though, is a special case. Johnson’s offense represents creativity and detail, born from a self-made coaching career. Flores’ defense embodies a trademark fearlessness. The Vikings don’t blitz because it’s flashy or because it produces eye-popping graphics. They send waves of bodies at offenses from all sides because that’s what they think is most likely to produce the right result.
Johnson has publicly stated his preference for points and blowouts. Flores makes no bones about his desire to apply a vise grip to opposing offenses. Neither settles for satisfaction. Both recognize the challenge the other presents.
“They do a great job,” Flores said Tuesday afternoon. “There’s shifts, there’s motions, there’s a lot of eye candy. They do everything that could potentially give a defense problems.”
He even offered a window into how his mind might work Sunday at Soldier Field. Employ one deep safety, and Chicago’s wideouts may feast against man-to-man coverage. Shift and feature two deep safeties, and the Bears could find susceptibilities in Minnesota’s ability to stop the run.
And that’s only the tip of the iceberg.
Safety positioning matters, but so do protection rules and pre-snap signals and down-and-distance tendencies. Each coverage choice comes with a cost. Different run concepts open the door to holes. All avenues of communication matter because they could contain the key for either side to decipher the deception.
As former Vikings defensive lineman Harrison Phillips put it several years ago, playing Johnson is like navigating a volatile stock market. You enter with expectations, but every drive seems like a forecasting exercise. Does it make sense to sell off while ahead? Should Minnesota adjust schematically even if the team is succeeding? Or does it make sense to stick with the investment? Should Minnesota maintain its approach, betting against Chicago’s ability to find a quick answer?
The shared history only adds to the complexity of the decisions.
“Each week, you try to find a weakness in the armor and look to attack it,” Johnson said ahead of the highly anticipated Vikings-Lions bout in Week 18 of the 2024 season. “This defense doesn’t have much, and it’s been that way for two years now. You can tell that this whole unit has been together. They have the answers. They know how to respond when they get hit with something.”
Going back to Johnson and Flores’ first faceoffs in 2023, a visual breakdown of the quarter-by-quarter efficiency statistics looks like a round-by-round scoring of Hagler-Hearns. Throwing the uppercut is less important than being able to absorb one.
In the Week 7 confrontation between Johnson’s Lions and Flores’ Vikings in 2024, Minnesota limited Detroit to a minuscule 21.4 percent success rate in the first quarter. Detroit answered with a ridiculous 61.1 percent success rate in the second quarter. The Lions kept their momentum with a 54.5 percent success rate in the third quarter, but the Vikings eliminated the rhythm by holding them to a 27.8 percent success rate in the fourth.
Detroit won 31-29, but the lopsided blow-by-blow revealed the ingenuity of their staffs and players.
Both coaches worked with a collective to identify and solve problems on the fly. This takes sharp eyes from above, intricate sideline dialogue and shrewd on-field adaptation.
“Any type of offense that’s out there — ground and pound, run and shoot, RPO, 4 by 1 — he’s got it,” Flores said. “So what are we getting this week? It’s hard to know. A lot of the game is adjustments. If they do this, we want to do this. We’re going to have our own game plan, and it’s the same on his end with him asking, ‘What are they doing? How are we going to counteract it?’”
Last year against Flores, Johnson utilized condensed formations, quick snaps and third-down runs at a notable clip. Flores, meanwhile, kept his max-pressure calls to a minimum against Johnson. He also deployed mostly zone coverage out of heavier personnel to neutralize the Bears’ run-pass multiplicity.
Also like poker players, they understand the others’ preferences. They know what moves the other prefers to make on the field.
“It’s one of the things I love about coaching defense in this division in the NFC,” Flores said. “It’s a lot of fun.”
It’s fun to watch, as well.

FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — During a break in their August joint practice, Philadelphia Eagles star running back Saquon Barkley asked his former teammate and current New England Patriots defensive tackle Milton Williams a question he and his teammates have grown familiar with, especially after their run to the Super Bowl a year ago.
What’s Mike Vrabel really
full_text:
Despite coming across as a hard-nosed, in-your-face leader, Patriots coach Mike Vrabel has embraced sports science. Jane Gershovich / Getty Images
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — During a break in their August joint practice, Philadelphia Eagles star running back Saquon Barkley asked his former teammate and current New England Patriots defensive tackle Milton Williams a question he and his teammates have grown familiar with, especially after their run to the Super Bowl a year ago.
What’s Mike Vrabel really like?
Opposing players have watched him run back to the locker room after games to be the first to hug his players. They’ve seen him run out onto the field every time a player is injured. And they’re often curious to hear a first-hand perspective on the 51-year-old coach.
Williams’ answer to Barkley revealed something surprising: The kid who grew up in football-mad, blue-collar Northeast Ohio , the former Ohio State linebacker who was part of the last generation of NFL players who went through grueling two-a-days, the hard-nosed, in-your-face leader who dives headfirst into fights … that guy is at the forefront of NFL coaches embracing sports science and load management.
“Vrabes, he used to play, so he be taking care of us,” Williams told Barkley .
It’s such a shocking twist for a coach who played for Bill Belichick, the “ No days off! ” guy , that it even confounds his new players.
A few days into training camp, they told fullback Reggie Gilliam he’d have the next day off. A “vet day,” it was called. Instead of practicing in full pads, the veteran of 95 NFL games was told to lift weights, spend some time riding a stationary bike and call it a day.
Gilliam was so taken aback that he called his mom right away to share the news.
“I was like, ‘You’re never going to believe this, but I just got my first-ever vet day,’” Gilliam said.
There’s more to it than simply letting an older player kick his feet up. All players wear a GPS tracking device during practices and games. The Patriots’ sports performance team, led by Frank Piraino, combs through the GPS numbers to determine who may need a breather.
They also develop long-term plans for older players, like right tackle Morgan Moses, who is in his 13th NFL season and is preparing for his 185th career game Sunday when the Patriots take on the Pittsburgh Steelers.
When Moses signed with the Patriots as a free agent 18 months ago, he had missed time in back-to-back seasons due to injuries. But with a plan spearheaded by Vrabel’s staff, Moses played in all 21 Patriots games (including the playoffs and Super Bowl) last season.
“It’s been something that I’ve had to learn,” Moses said of his load management plan that includes taking it easy during some practices. “Especially as an offensive lineman, you want to be out there every play. We never get a break during the game. …
“But he’s a great coach and was a great player in this league for a long time. You trust that whatever he has planned for you is the best for you.”
It’s not just Moses who has seen results. The Patriots were one of the league’s healthiest teams last year during their run to Super Bowl LX.
Still, injuries are unavoidable in football. A.J. Brown will miss around six games after suffering a high ankle sprain when a cornerback’s knee landed on his ankle in Week 1. TreVeyon Henderson is working his way back from an ankle injury in practice.
But Vrabel is looking to limit the injuries that come from wear and tear and exhaustion on the field. It’s a surprising turn for a coach whose preseason preparations during his playing career included practicing in full pads twice a day. Does any part of him miss those days?
“No, I thought 10 straight two-a-days was a good way to prepare the football team,” Vrabel joked when confronted with that dynamic. “I just think as the data becomes more available, you have to be careful (not) to go overboard. You want to track certain numbers, high-speed numbers, yardage and all the other stuff and also have a pretty good gauge of the player and what they look like and how conditioned they are. And we try to set the schedule up accordingly. …
“When there is a longer stretch (of consecutive practices or games), you may have to dial back on a particular player. But I think when you become a head coach, you try to focus on the things that get the team ready and what each guy needs. And then some more of the GPS stuff became really popular and prevalent, and anything that can help us keep the players out there, I’m all for.”
Of course, load management has existed in other sports for years. It’s common practice for NBA players to sit out not just practices but regular-season games to keep their bodies fresh. It’s similar in Major League Baseball.
It’s a newer idea in football, though Vrabel is certainly not alone in trying to minimize the injury risk for established players.
“He’s got a good feel for when guys are hurting,” Williams said. “We’ll still practice, but he knows when to take a load off of us. He’s going to take care of us when he feels like we need it, but also when it’s time to practice and it’s time to go, (he will say), ‘I need it all from you.’”
As for the formula that decides who gets the valued days off from practice? That’s secret and takes into account a player’s recent workload, injury history and the depth behind him at that position.
So even though Williams, 27, is one of the team’s top players, no one from coaching or training staff has approached him (and his 80 career games) about load management.
“I guess I haven’t been in the league long enough yet,” Williams said with a laugh. “I don’t know how close I am to that.”

full_text:
The NFL Projection Model thinks quarterback Jaxson Dart and the New York Giants will be a factor in the NFC playoff race. Julian Leshay Guadalupe / Imagn Images
Should we overreact to Week 1 results? Tell me this: Should we have cared that the Las Vegas Raiders beat the AFC champion New England Patriots in Week 1 last year?
The answer to both questions is, of course, no.
However, just because we don’t want to overreact to a small sample size doesn’t mean there’s nothing to learn from the first week of NFL action. We spent all offseason talking about coach movement, free-agent signings, draft picks, and trades, and we finally got to see teams’ plans — or lack thereof, in some cases — in action, which means there are plenty of data points worth discussing.
So while we shouldn’t overreact, we’ll use my NFL Projection Model to guide us toward some things we saw play out in Week 1 that we think are real, as well as a couple that aren’t.
Put more simply: These are five things we saw in Week 1 that the model is buying or selling.
Maybe the Dallas Cowboys’ problematic defense isn’t any better than last year, but the New York Giants absolutely destroyed them from wire to wire Sunday night; it was the kind of performance that often predicts future success. Perhaps the most impressive aspect of the offense was quarterback Jaxson Dart’s play . Dart made some nice throws, took what the Cowboys gave him, and used his legs effectively. I’m not sure I was fully bought into the Dart experience within a Matt Nagy and Greg Roman offense, but the poise and accuracy he showed in prime time has me reconsidering that stance.
Outside of Dart, the other reason the model likes the Giants more today than it did before the season is that they looked better than expected in the trenches. The Giants’ offensive line completely dominated the Cowboys’ front, delivering 0.7 EPA per dropback and a 51 percent success rate on the ground. The model still has concerns about New York’s defense, but it’s buying the offense being better than expected and believes the Giants will be a factor in the NFC playoff race.
Playoff odds before Week 1 : 14 percent • Today : 33 percent
Yes, the New England Patriots blew a game where the Seattle Seahawks lost their starting quarterback very early and the offense looked out of sorts. Oh, and they lost A.J. Brown for at least four games with a high ankle sprain. But my model won’t penalize an offense for struggling on the road in Seattle against a Mike Macdonald defense; that’s no easy task for any quarterback.
The model is also buying Drake Maye being just fine, and the defense is too good to panic after one game against one of the better teams in the NFL. How they fare without Brown will likely determine the course of their season. Maybe they won’t be on the same level as the Bills for the AFC East title, but with the Bengals, Broncos, and Chargers looking less than impressive in Week 1, I think the Patriots are more than likely to make the playoffs despite the early loss — and the model agrees.
Playoff odds before Week 1 : 74 percent • Today : 57 percent
There is little reason to doubt coach Matt LaFleur’s abilities as a play caller or quarterback Jordan Love’s ability to execute LaFleur’s offense. We have plenty of historical data showing both are good at those things. Unfortunately, the Green Bay Packers’ offensive line is in shambles, and it will be extremely tough for them to overcome that.
Everything looked good through three quarters against the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, mostly because of explosive plays, but things changed dramatically in the fourth quarter. Vikings’ defensive coordinator Brian Flores clearly figured out the Packers’ protection and orchestrated five QB pressures, two sacks, two turnovers, and six negative plays on 11 five-man pressures in the final period. The Packers had no answer for Flores’ attack, and the offense disintegrated. Perhaps the problem was facing a Flores defense, which they won’t do every week, but the model is concerned this is the start of a bad trend for Green Bay.
On the other side of the ball, the Packers’ defense will struggle until star pass rusher Micah Parsons returns from injury. Maybe LaFleur and Love can mask the offensive line issues, but my model puts the Packers’ playoff odds at just 30 percent, and Parsons won’t be on the field for another month. Frankly, I think they are in danger of losing this weekend against the maybe-not-so-lowly New York Jets.
Playoff odds before Week 1 : 52 percent • Today : 30 percent
This might be an unpopular take, and it might blow up in my face, but despite the 31 points, I wasn’t all that impressed by the Detroit Lions offense on Sunday against the New Orleans Saints. They managed just a 43 percent success rate through the air against a Saints defense that was pretty thin along the defensive line. The Lions are in a transition period on the offensive line, and it’s hard to love what we saw Sunday.
Sure, they posted 31 points, but they also had 13 drives, excluding kneel-downs. Eight of those drives didn’t amount to more than 18 yards; four were three-and-outs and two of their touchdown drives started in plus territory. Running back Jahmyr Gibbs is fantastic, and he was awesome on Sunday, but if they can’t throw the ball efficiently — again, the Saints were thin on defense — I’m not sure they’ll have enough juice in a crowded NFC North.
Playoff odds before Week 1 : 67 percent • Today : 73 percent
When quarterback Lamar Jackson faked a handoff and called his own number for the Baltimore Ravens’ first touchdown of the year on Sunday, I couldn’t think anything but, “That’s MVP Lamar.” For the rest of the game, he seemed to play with a different level of burst and aggressiveness than last season, when he dealt with nagging injuries. Obviously, getting MVP-caliber quarterback play will give any team a good shot at being elite, but I thought the entire offense looked great. Running game, passing game, all of it. New offensive coordinator Declan Doyle seems like he learned a lot as coach Ben Johnson’s understudy in Chicago last year.
LAMAR JACKSON TOUCHDOWN!!!
Tune in on @NFLonCBS and @ParamountPlus . pic.twitter.com/kEqwpqd2gG
— Baltimore Ravens (@Ravens) September 13, 2026
Meanwhile, on the defensive side of the ball, new coach Jesse Minter’s impact was seen right away; same goes for new pass rusher Trey Hendrickson. Now, there’s real concern for the Ravens’ pass-catching group, as Zay Flowers (hamstring) and Ja’Kobi Lane (fractured wrist) are expected to miss some time. However, given how good Jackson looked on Sunday, I’m not that concerned.
Playoff odds before Week 1 : 83 percent • Today : 95 percent

The answer to both questions is, of course, no.
However, just because we don’t want to overreact to a small sample size doesn’t mean there’s nothing to learn from the first week of NFL action. We spent all offseason talking about coach movement, free-agent signings, draft picks, and trades, and we finally got to see teams’ plans — or lack thereof, in some cases — in action, which means there are plenty of data points worth discussing.
So while we shouldn’t overreact, we’ll use my NFL Projection Model to guide us toward some things we saw play out in Week 1 that we think are real, as well as a couple that aren’t.
Put more simply: These are five things we saw in Week 1 that the model is buying or selling.
Maybe the Dallas Cowboys’ problematic defense isn’t any better than last year, but the New York Giants absolutely destroyed them from wire to wire Sunday night; it was the kind of performance that often predicts future success. Perhaps the most impressive aspect of the offense was quarterback Jaxson Dart’s play . Dart made some nice throws, took what the Cowboys gave him, and used his legs effectively. I’m not sure I was fully bought into the Dart experience within a Matt Nagy and Greg Roman offense, but the poise and accuracy he showed in prime time has me reconsidering that stance.
Outside of Dart, the other reason the model likes the Giants more today than it did before the season is that they looked better than expected in the trenches. The Giants’ offensive line completely dominated the Cowboys’ front, delivering 0.7 EPA per dropback and a 51 percent success rate on the ground. The model still has concerns about New York’s defense, but it’s buying the offense being better than expected and believes the Giants will be a factor in the NFC playoff race.
Playoff odds before Week 1 : 14 percent • Today : 33 percent
Yes, the New England Patriots blew a game where the Seattle Seahawks lost their starting quarterback very early and the offense looked out of sorts. Oh, and they lost A.J. Brown for at least four games with a high ankle sprain. But my model won’t penalize an offense for struggling on the road in Seattle against a Mike Macdonald defense; that’s no easy task for any quarterback.
The model is also buying Drake Maye being just fine, and the defense is too good to panic after one game against one of the better teams in the NFL. How they fare without Brown will likely determine the course of their season. Maybe they won’t be on the same level as the Bills for the AFC East title, but with the Bengals, Broncos, and Chargers looking less than impressive in Week 1, I think the Patriots are more than likely to make the playoffs despite the early loss — and the model agrees.
Playoff odds before Week 1 : 74 percent • Today : 57 percent
There is little reason to doubt coach Matt LaFleur’s abilities as a play caller or quarterback Jordan Love’s ability to execute LaFleur’s offense. We have plenty of historical data showing both are good at those things. Unfortunately, the Green Bay Packers’ offensive line is in shambles, and it will be extremely tough for them to overcome that.
Everything looked good through three quarters against the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, mostly because of explosive plays, but things changed dramatically in the fourth quarter. Vikings’ defensive coordinator Brian Flores clearly figured out the Packers’ protection and orchestrated five QB pressures, two sacks, two turnovers, and six negative plays on 11 five-man pressures in the final period. The Packers had no answer for Flores’ attack, and the offense disintegrated. Perhaps the problem was facing a Flores defense, which they won’t do every week, but the model is concerned this is the start of a bad trend for Green Bay.
On the other side of the ball, the Packers’ defense will struggle until star pass rusher Micah Parsons returns from injury. Maybe LaFleur and Love can mask the offensive line issues, but my model puts the Packers’ playoff odds at just 30 percent, and Parsons won’t be on the field for another month. Frankly, I think they are in danger of losing this weekend against the maybe-not-so-lowly New York Jets.
Playoff odds before Week 1 : 52 percent • Today : 30 percent
This might be an unpopular take, and it might blow up in my face, but despite the 31 points, I wasn’t all that impressed by the Detroit Lions offense on Sunday against the New Orleans Saints. They managed just a 43 percent success rate through the air against a Saints defense that was pretty thin along the defensive line. The Lions are in a transition period on the offensive line, and it’s hard to love what we saw Sunday.
Sure, they posted 31 points, but they also had 13 drives, excluding kneel-downs. Eight of those drives didn’t amount to more than 18 yards; four were three-and-outs and two of their touchdown drives started in plus territory. Running back Jahmyr Gibbs is fantastic, and he was awesome on Sunday, but if they can’t throw the ball efficiently — again, the Saints were thin on defense — I’m not sure they’ll have enough juice in a crowded NFC North.
Playoff odds before Week 1 : 67 percent • Today : 73 percent
When quarterback Lamar Jackson faked a handoff and called his own number for the Baltimore Ravens’ first touchdown of the year on Sunday, I couldn’t think anything but, “That’s MVP Lamar.” For the rest of the game, he seemed to play with a different level of burst and aggressiveness than last season, when he dealt with nagging injuries. Obviously, getting MVP-caliber quarterback play will give any team a good shot at being elite, but I thought the entire offense looked great. Running game, passing game, all of it. New offensive coordinator Declan Doyle seems like he learned a lot as coach Ben Johnson’s understudy in Chicago last year.
LAMAR JACKSON TOUCHDOWN!!!
Tune in on @NFLonCBS and @ParamountPlus . pic.twitter.com/kEqwpqd2gG
— Baltimore Ravens (@Ravens) September 13, 2026
Meanwhile, on the defensive side of the ball, new coach Jesse Minter’s impact was seen right away; same goes for new pass rusher Trey Hendrickson. Now, there’s real concern for the Ravens’ pass-catching group, as Zay Flowers (hamstring) and Ja’Kobi Lane (fractured wrist) are expected to miss some time. However, given how good Jackson looked on Sunday, I’m not that concerned.

title: Eagles’ Moro Ojomo keeps making plays — and a name for himself A late Week 1 stop showed why the Eagles value Moro Ojomo (MORE-oh oh-JOE-moh), who could be a top free agent in 2027. Zach Berman 4
summary:
Moro Ojomo (97) helped secure the Eagles’ Week 1 win by stopping Washington’s 2-point conversion attempt late in the fourth quarter. Michael Owens / Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — The pronunciation was perfect. Moro Ojomo with the big play, and the Eagles make the stand they needed!
That’s what a national audience heard after Ojomo’s lead-saving tackle in the fourth quarter of the Philadelphia Eagles’ win over the Washington Commanders. Ojomo’s name was pronounced as spelled in the team’s pronuncia
full_text:
Moro Ojomo (97) helped secure the Eagles’ Week 1 win by stopping Washington’s 2-point conversion attempt late in the fourth quarter. Michael Owens / Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — The pronunciation was perfect. Moro Ojomo with the big play, and the Eagles make the stand they needed!
That’s what a national audience heard after Ojomo’s lead-saving tackle in the fourth quarter of the Philadelphia Eagles’ win over the Washington Commanders. Ojomo’s name was pronounced as spelled in the team’s pronunciation guide: “MORE-oh oh-JOE-moh.”
Had that same tackle occurred during Week 1 of the 2024 season, the pronunciation would have been different. It would have been: “MOH-roh uh-JUH-muh.” He used that pronunciation when he entered the NFL to better reflect the Nigerian pronunciation. During the 2024 postseason, Ojomo asked the team to change it to match the version used in college at Texas. He became a bigger contributor and even recorded his first sack that winter.
He heard his name discussed more often. The pronunciations were seldom correct.
“They butchered it,” Ojomo explained last season. “I felt like it would be something easier for them to say.”
Ojomo offered a reporter the correct way to pronounce his name, with phonetics natural to his native Nigeria. The pronunciation guide see-sawed during his time with the Eagles.
What’s become clear: You should know his name, because it’s not going away.
Moro Ojomo with a big time stop on the 2-pt conversion 😤
WASvsPHI on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/4xlQSvcuZp
— NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026
Ojomo shares a position group with two of the NFL’s 10 highest-paid defensive tackles. Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis were first-round picks who signed lucrative contract extensions this offseason.
Ojomo is “proud and happy” for his teammates. He also refuses to take a back seat.
“I’m always trying to be the best,” Ojomo said this summer. “We have an extremely loaded room. Those guys know I’m not backing down from anything. The goal is always to be the best defensive tackle, and that’s the mindset. I want to make more plays, I want to have more sacks, I want to make more TFLs, I want to be the best in the room and the best in the league.”
Ojomo’s talent is no secret in the Eagles locker room — or the NFL. Ojomo played 66 percent of the defensive snaps last season and finished second on the team with six sacks. On Sunday, he played 69 percent of the defensive snaps and thwarted the Commanders’ two-point conversion attempt to tie the game in the fourth quarter when he spun away from a block and upended the ball carrier on a shovel pass short of the end zone.
Ojomo said he saw the guard pull and anticipated the play — “You can’t play indecisive,” he said — and the sequence was more than the right place at the right time.
“I think part of it is due to his effort,” defensive coordinator Vic Fangio said. “His dogged effort plays a part in that, which he’s a little undersized as D-tackles go, and he needs to have all that stuff working for him. But he does have good instincts, but he gives great effort and he’s tenacious.
“They hadn’t shown that (play). Obviously, that was a special play they had cooked up for a 2-point play, and it was more of his reaction and instincts after the ball was snapped than anything pre-snap.”
During an interview late last season, Ojomo explained that his biggest growth came with understanding and dissecting offenses, knowing how to attack different plays and players. It led to the type of stops he made Sunday.
When the Eagles hired defensive line coach Clint Hurtt before the 2024 season, Ojomo was the first player to visit his office. At the time, Ojomo was an emerging second-year player on a crowded depth chart with only 68 snaps as a rookie. “You could feel his presence and his hunger to get better,” Hurtt said. Hurtt learned that quest had no end. Ojomo’s curiosity and intensity require the coach to never set a limit — and never lack an answer.
“Giving him the ‘why’ for everything — he needs to know the full picture,” Hurtt said. “The speed and the process of his development has happened because of that eagerness to go and learn.”
Ojomo oozed upside as a seventh-round pick in 2023 who entered the building as a 21-year-old fifth-year senior after enrolling at Texas at age 16. Ojomo acknowledged that “potential” defined his career until last season, when he moved into a more prominent role after Milton Williams signed a $104 million contract with the New England Patriots. Before the 2025 campaign, Hurtt pulled Ojomo aside in the weight room and said he needed to start preparing for success and praise. “I knew this was coming,” Hurtt explained.
He wanted to ensure Ojomo did not lose “all the things that make you great — your humility, your eagerness to learn, the work ethic.” Those might seem like intangibles. Hurtt saw them as differentiators, similar to the attributes Fangio identified with the 2-point stop Sunday.
“His effort — I know that may seem like a simple thing, but that’s a valuable trait that not every player masters, because it is a skill,” Hurtt said. “Playing hard is a skill. … Not everybody does it. If you’re in the real world at a Fortune 500 company, the people who get retained and that you want to make sure you have as long as you possibly can are the people who grind and know how to work. … You can harp on it all you want to, but when you find somebody who innately has it within them, that’s a skill that, to me, is priceless.”
There’s definitely a price for Ojomo. The league will soon show it. The Eagles will soon realize it.
“Howie (Roseman) needs to save some money for him, too,” Fangio said in July of the 2027 free agent.
Even though Ojomo is the third defensive tackle, he’s considered a starter and plays a high volume of snaps. He could be one of the market’s top free agents in March. Ojomo deferred contract questions to his agent — “If I try to do his job for him, I’d be a worse player,” Ojomo said — but he also knows what’s at stake this season. Fangio said Ojomo has “already been a good player here,” and the Eagles “expect that and even a little bit more.”
Ojomo shared a lesson from his father about “never having a worse yesterday.” The objective is steady improvement, each day independent of the next.
“I think he’s going to have an amazing season,” Hurtt said this summer. “Coaching him is an absolute pleasure. Having Moro, super, super smart, great communicator, the vocal leader of the group. I think they all lead in their own specific way, but he’s very outspoken, and that speaks to the confidence that he has in himself. But I think he’s gonna have a phenomenal year.”
Hurtt said in January that Ojomo has Pro Bowl potential, can consistently produce seven or eight sacks a season and even reach double digits. It’s similar upside to Williams before he signed a nine-digit deal. Williams told reporters in August that Ojomo’s “future is bright.” The two keep in touch. Ojomo stepped in for Williams.
And somebody might soon need to step in for Ojomo. That might be a story for March. Before then, he’s a key player on the Eagles defense — and one who already made a key play in an Eagles victory.
“Milt didn’t get as much opportunity until that last year, and he took it and ran with it,” Ojomo said. “That’s the mindset. He’s a hard worker and he played hard. You look back, even all the way to (Javon) Hargrave, the Eagles have had a history of DTs doing really well and ending up somewhere else.”
Inside the Eagles’ building, they call Ojomo “Mo.”
“I call him ‘Coach Mo,'” Davis said.
Ojomo has put thought into what the public should call him. Last November, he said he even considered going by his full name: Morotoluwa.
“It means standing with God,” Ojomo said.
In high school, a long name annoyed him. He has since wondered if using his full name would make a similar kid watching him feel more secure. He also acknowledged that, when considering the different pronunciations,…

title: The Cardinals Are Suddenly Leaning on the NFL's Most Confusing Defense
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals were at the forefront of shocking headlines in Week 1 after stunning the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium.
Mike LaFleur's offense expectedly stole the show in their 26-14 win. Arizona's attack looked much improved compared to prior seasons through both the ground and air.
The defense ultimately proved to be the difference (which is something we already covered ) — though the Cardinals ran one coverage more than the entire NFL in Week 1: Cover 6. The Cardinals' 42.9% usage rate of the zone scheme ranked first across the league according to Football Insights:
Defensive coverage rates in Week 1 Via @FantasyPtsData pic.twitter.com/YAAYNFielQ
What is it? What makes Cover 6 so desirable, and what does it tell us about the Cardinals?
In a complex league, defensive coverages are mostly broken down into sub sections: man and zone defense.
When running man coverage, defenders follow one offensive player across the field regardless of where they go. In zone, defenders are simply responsible for a certain area of the field as opposed to a specific player.
Some modern defenses will sometimes blend variations of two defenses and can be change based off matchups/personnel, but we're here to learn basic match — not calculus.
Zone defense can be split into four different coverages: Cover 2 (which can also be used in man), Cover 3, Cover 4 and Cover 6. Each defense has various pros and cons to its respective zone setup, and as you could guess, each number describes the number of deep zones covered by the defense.
Remember how we're avoiding calculus? Cover 6 is just a tad below that but above basic math, so we'll call this algebra. Cover 6 is a combination of Cover 2 on one side of the field with the other half playing Cover 4. It operates with two high safeties and has one boundary corner rolling deep to ultimately create three deep zones while the opposite corner stays in the flat.
Teams mostly play the Cover 2 half towards the strong/passing advantage side of the offense with Cover 4 being played on the backside.
here's what typical Seahawks Cover 6 (QQH) looks like on 3rd & XL against 3x1 looks. pic.twitter.com/KQw6qVa8zq
Got it? Probably not! NFL quarterbacks have a tough time digesting it, too. It's a tough cookie to crumble, and that's why Cardinals defensive coordinator Nick Rallis loves it.
Rallis' defense has often been described as complex, from the players executing the system itself to opposing coaches who have to gameplan for it during the week.
Rallis isn't inherently aggressive in nature. The Cardinals ranked near the middle of the table in blitz percentage last season while Week 1 saw him send pressure on just 20% of plays, which ranked second to last on Sunday.
By no means is he Brian Flores, but he opts for confusion post-snap, and that's where the heavy Cover 6 comes into play.
Quarterbacks try to identify coverages before the ball is snapped. While modern defenses have gotten better at disguising what they'll do, there's certain tells that can tip a passer on whether they're throwing against man, zone, a certain coverage, etc.
That's half the battle for a quarterback — knowing where to attack — though Cover 6 disrupts that evaluation process both pre and post-snap. Defenders can show vastly different alignments before the play and by splitting the field into two entirely different looks post-snap, progressions are much harder to successfully move through.
The data backs that up, too. According to Sumer Sports, Cover 6 had the highest interception rate of any coverage last season.
Removing prevent snaps from the 2025 regular season, Cover 6 had the highest interception rate of any coverage, per @SumerSports 1. Cover 6: 2.63% 2. Cover 0: 2.54% 3. Cover 3: 2.22% 4. Cover 2: 2.15% 5. Cover 4: 2.03% 6. Cover 1: 2.01% 7. 2 Man: 1.29%
Rallis' creativity and hopes to disguise can thrive in Cover 6 due to the various different ways the two respective sides of the field can be deployed within the defense.
That hesitation from the quarterback isn't only great for interceptions – the delay in decisionmaking can increase pressure and lead to more sacks. Such was the case on Sunday, as a Cardinals pass rush tallied three sacks on Justin Herbert with Josh Sweat not being a factor.
Of course, there's weaknesses to running Cover 6 so often. For as much as two-high safety looks have dominated the league in recent years, only ten teams ran the look more than 20% of their defensive snaps this past week.
Perhaps the biggest issue lies within its strengths. It's tough for an offense to diagnose Cover 6, but it's equally tough on the defenders running it. The amount of football IQ, communication and recognition it takes to successfully implement Cover 6 is high.
One of the biggest complaints around Rallis' defensive units is the amount of missed assignments, where communication breaks down and guys are left open. Dialing up Cover 6 only threatens those problems more while also being considered strong against the run.
From an x's and o's standpoint, Cover 6 has weaknesses in the flats and the "hole" between the boundary corner and safety. Deep ball success isn't often against Cover 6, though running a seam/streak and post pattern attacking the Cover 2 side can create problems as well.
This coverage isn't unbeatable — nothing is — and Rallis shouldn't use it as some sort of elixir to cover all of Arizona's defensive problems. Like any other scheme/play in the NFL, it will eventually be figured out.
However, his deployment of such a sophisticated scheme led to success in Week 1, and it'll be interesting to see how the Cardinals move forward as film begins to build and offenses become sharper.

title: Ex-Cardinals OLB BJ Ojulari Lands New Opportunity
full_text:
ARIZONA — Arizona Cardinals outside linebacker BJ Ojulari was one of the team's biggest roster cuts ahead of the regular season. Now, after a few weeks, he's found a new home.
According to NFL insider Jordan Schultz, the Jacksonville Jaguars are signing Ojulari.
Sources: The #Jaguars are signing former #Cardinals OLB BJ Ojulari. Still just 24 years old, Ojulari was a 2nd-round pick in 2023 out of LSU. pic.twitter.com/D9ZA0Kmf6B
Ojulari arrived to the desert with high hopes of reaching the quarterback after a successful college stint at LSU, which made him a second-round pick. His length made him an attractive edge player for the Cardinals in general manager Monti Ossenfort's first draft running the show.
Ojulari generated plenty of buzz during his rookie season, tallying four sacks and setting the stage for what many had hoped to be a second-year leap.
However, a severe knee injury suffered during training camp derailed those hopes. Ojulari would miss the entire 2024 season and the first half of 2025 before he eventually returned. In the eight games he played last year, Ojulari notched one sack with three quarterback hits and nine tackles.
Entering this summer, all eyes were on Ojulari to see how he would look finally entering a training camp at full health. Ojulari failed to make an impact in a fairly set Cardinals edge room, and his participation deep into every preseason game signaled Arizona was eying other options in the room.
That ultimately proved to be true, as underdog outside linebacker Eku Leota made the Cardinals' final 53-man roster over Ojulari, sending the fourth-year edge rusher to find a new team.
"We made a decision based on what we felt was best, and I feel for BJ," Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur told reporters after roster cuts.
"If you guys saw the work that he put in behind the scenes to try to get back to the level that he knows he's capable of, you'd root for him too. And his journey and his story is not over. But that was a rough injury that he went through, and in my six months here, however long I've been, all I saw was a guy that had his shoulders up and his head held high, and he just attacked it."
That was weeks ago, and now with Week 1 fully under our belts, the Jaguars decided to pull the trigger on adding Ojulari to a room that holds former Cardinals linebacker Dennis Gardeck. Ojulari was likely signed to help replace edge rusher BJ Green, who left Week 1 with an elbow injury.

title: 5 Advanced Stats Reveal the Real Story of Cardinals' Week 1 Upset — And Maybe What's Next
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals won their season opener in Los Angeles, and now, all eyes look ahead to a daunting home opener that will welcome the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks to State Farm Stadium.
Box scores, unfortunately, will only tell a small part of the story.
These five stats lay out a bigger picture of how the Cardinals won against the Chargers, and what could be in store ahead:
Brissett's time to throw was the second lowest out of all quarterbacks on Sunday, trailing just Joe Burrow. The 2.56 second mark was also tied with Jordan Love, who was blitzed on 80% of snaps.
What's to make of this? This could be a mix of Brissett being quick through his progressions and a lack of protecting, which we'll get into here in a second. This also may have been intentional in the game plan by head coach Mike LaFleur.
“Yeah, I thought [QB] Jacoby [Brissett] did a heck of a job on getting the ball out, when they were starting to bring some pressure and stuff like that," LaFleur said post-game.
Chargers defensive coordinator Chris O'Leary blitzed on only 20% of snaps, so it's not as if Brissett was under fire the entire game like Love was.
Still, it's interesting Brissett had the ball out nearly faster than everybody in the NFL on Sunday.
This may be a piece to that puzzle we just talked about.
The Cardinals' pass block win rate of 22% ranked second-worst in the league according to ESPN. They only ranked ahead of the Green Bay Packers at 9%.
Brissett was sacked just once on the afternoon while he was hurried on just 7.7% of plays, which ranked dead middle of the league after Week 1. While Chargers defenders didn't quite get home all day, advanced analytics clearly indicate the Cardinals' offensive line was worrisome.
Paris Johnson finished with a 79.3 grade on Pro Football Focus while none of the other four Cardinals starting offensive linemen finished above 65.
This is certainly something to watch moving forward.
One of the main expectations around the Cardinals under LaFleur was a heavy dose of 13 personnel thanks to his prior team (Rams) using it at eye-opening rates last season. In Week 1, Arizona was one of five NFL teams to use three tight end packages at a rate of 20% or higher.
For those curious, the Bills (50%) and Rams (40%) led the way.
This number could jump when tight end Tip Reiman is eventually off injured reserve, as he's an excellent run blocker and could elevate Arizona's rushing attack to new heights. However, the fact that the Cardinals are still using the packaging at such high rates without a key piece is encouraging.
Rallis' blitz rate on Sunday was the second-lowest across the league — trailing only Patrick Graham's 10.5% rate.
The fact that Arizona was able to hold the Chargers to 14 points and sack Herbert three times without being fully aggressive is telling of a few things.
The Cardinals were able to execute their bend but don't break defense incredibly after L.A.'s opening drive. Arizona also was more than content to only rush four players and drop seven more into coverage.
Whether that translates over the next few weeks remains to be seen, though the Cardinals' defense was impactful while being conservative.
Part of keeping the Chargers' offense to just 14 points was they simply didn't have the ball a lot.
Los Angeles trailed the possession game by a whopping 15 minutes to Arizona. Yes, the Cardinals had the ball for an entire quarter's worth of play over the Chargers.
That speaks to Arizona's ability to continually move the chains while churning clock late in the game. When the Cardinals needed to squeeze some minutes out of their final possessions, they were able to hand the ball off and kept the clock ticking.
It's awfully hard for Chargers offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel to scheme up plays if his quarterback's sitting on the sideline for long durations of time.
LaFleur's offense looks night and day different from the 2025 Cardinals that fans grew so tired of seeing. Complementary football is demanded if you're going to win at the NFL level, and the saying of "the best defense is a good option" very much was true at SoFi Stadium.
